::: {.callout-tip}
#### Learning objectives
- Build subcellular spatial maps of classification results with `plot2D`, and
  compare different dimensionality reduction methods (`plot2Dmethods`).
- Pre-compute PCA, t-SNE, UMAP and LDA coordinates (`plot = FALSE`) and reuse
  them (`method = "none"`) for efficient, reproducible figures.
- Summarise the characteristic profile of each compartment with
  `mrkConsProfiles`, `mrkHClust` and `plotConsProfiles`.
- Overlay peptide support and missing values on spatial maps, both for the
  combined data and for each replicate, and relate them to classification
  results.
- Find members of protein complexes by gene name, highlight them on spatial
  maps (`highlightOnPlot`), and add them as new `fData` annotations
  (`addMarkers`).
- Compare the profiles of proteins of interest with those of their
  compartment (`plotDist`).
:::




## Introduction

In the previous lesson we classified the proteins in our U-2 OS data and
generated our first spatial maps. Our `msn` object now contains the curated
markers (`markers`), the thresholded SVM predictions (`svm.pred`), and the
quality columns we added to the joined set at the end of part 1 with
`addProfileQC()`: the number of precursors per protein in each replicate
(`n_rep1`, `n_rep2`, `n_rep3`) with their minimum (`n_min`), and the
proportion of values missing before imputation in each replicate
(`missing_rep1`, `missing_rep2`, `missing_rep3`) with their maximum
(`missing_max`).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Columns we will use in this lesson
msn |>
  fvarLabels()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

 [5] "Protein.Group"            "Protein.Names"

[11] "Channel.Q.Value"          "Lib.PG.Q.Value"

[17] "n_min"                    "n_mean"

[21] "missing_rep3"             "missing_max"

```


:::
:::


In this lesson we focus on visualisation: making spatial maps efficiently with
different dimensionality reduction methods, summarising compartment profiles,
showing peptide support and missing values, and overlaying protein complexes and other
annotations of interest.


## Spatial maps with different dimensionality reduction methods

The result of classification is a list of proteins and their predicted
subcellular localisations. These can be visualised as a "subcellular spatial
map" using `plot2D`, by passing the column containing the predictions to
`fcol`. In the previous lessons we mostly used PCA, the default. However,
`plot2D` supports several other methods, listed in `plot2Dmethods` (see
`?plot2D` for details).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot2Dmethods
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] "PCA"    "MDS"    "kpca"   "lda"    "t-SNE"  "UMAP"   "nipals" "hexbin"
 [9] "none"   "scree" 
```


:::
:::


Each method summarises the data in a different way, and no single method shows
everything. As discussed in the lesson on assessing resolution, PCA preserves
distances but only shows two components at a time, whereas non-linear methods
such as t-SNE and UMAP often separate clusters more clearly but distort
distances. It is therefore good practice to look at more than one.

### Pre-computing coordinates

Non-linear methods such as t-SNE and UMAP can take from a minute to tens of
minutes to compute on a dataset of this size. They are also stochastic, so
each run gives a slightly different picture unless we set a seed. Rather than
recomputing the coordinates every time we make a plot, it is good practice to
compute them once, with a seed, and reuse them.

To do this, we pass `plot = FALSE` to `plot2D`. Instead of drawing a plot,
`plot2D` then returns a matrix of the two-dimensional coordinates of each
protein. Below we pre-compute coordinates for PCA, UMAP, t-SNE and linear
discriminant analysis (LDA). LDA is a supervised method: it uses the markers
to find the projection that best separates the compartments.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## PCA is deterministic, so we do not need to set a seed
pcas <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "PCA", plot = FALSE)

## UMAP
set.seed(399)
umap <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "UMAP", plot = FALSE)

## t-SNE
set.seed(399)
tsne <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "t-SNE", plot = FALSE)

## Linear discriminant analysis (uses the markers column)
set.seed(399)
lda <- msn |>
  plot2D(method = "lda", plot = FALSE)
```
:::




Each object is a matrix with one row per protein and two columns.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
head(pcas)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
           PC1 (35.15%) PC2 (25.23%)
A0A096LP01    -2.811345   -5.2274624
A0A0B4J2F0    -2.377583   -5.4941955
A0A3B3IRV3     2.425945    1.4670772
A0A3B3IS91     5.156840   -0.3892221
A0AV96         4.093129    0.5750826
A0AVF1         4.644023   -0.2817537
```


:::
:::


### Plotting pre-computed coordinates

We can now pass these coordinates back to `plot2D` with `method = "none"`,
which tells `plot2D` not to compute anything. Because a matrix of coordinates
does not contain the feature data, we also pass our `MSnSet` to `methargs` so
that `plot2D` knows where to find the `fcol` annotation.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "PCA")
plot2D(umap, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "UMAP")
plot2D(tsne, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "t-SNE")
plot2D(lda, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "LDA")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "svm.pred", where = "topright", ncol = 2, cex = .7)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


The same compartments are found in all four maps, but each method shows them
differently. Compartments that overlap in the PCA plot may be clearly separated
in the t-SNE or UMAP plots, and vice versa. Remember that distances between
clusters in t-SNE and UMAP plots cannot be interpreted directly.


## Compartment fingerprints with `plotConsProfiles`

Spatial maps show where proteins lie relative to each other, but they hide the
profiles themselves. A compact way to summarise the profiles of a whole class
is to calculate its consensus profile, the average profile of the proteins in
that class, and display all of these together as a heatmap. Each row is a
compartment, each column a fraction, and the colour shows the consensus
profile. This gives a "fingerprint" of each compartment across the
fractionation gradient.

This takes three steps in `pRoloc`:

1. `mrkConsProfiles` calculates the consensus profile of each compartment and
   returns a matrix with one row per compartment and one column per fraction.
2. `mrkHClust` clusters the compartments by their consensus profiles. We use the
   resulting dendrogram to order the rows of the heatmap, so that compartments
   with similar profiles are next to each other.
3. `plotConsProfiles` plots the matrix as a heatmap, in the given order.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## 1. Consensus profile of each marker class
fmat <- mrkConsProfiles(msn, fcol = "markers")
dim(fmat)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 13 27
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
## 2. Order the classes by hierarchical clustering of their profiles
hc <- mrkHClust(msn, fcol = "markers", plot = FALSE)
mm <- getMarkerClasses(msn, fcol = "markers")
ord <- levels(factor(mm))[order.dendrogram(hc)]
ord
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] "Chromatin"     "Mitochondrion" "Golgi"         "Lysosome"     
 [5] "ER"            "PM"            "Endosome"      "Peroxisome"   
 [9] "Cytosol"       "Proteasome"    "Nucleus"       "Ribosome 40S" 
[13] "Ribosome 60S" 
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## 3. Plot the consensus profiles of the markers
plotConsProfiles(fmat, order = ord)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


Each compartment has a distinct fingerprint, with its abundance peaking in
different fractions, and the pattern is repeated in each of the three
replicates. Compartments next to each other in this plot have similar
fingerprints and are harder to separate, which is consistent with what we saw
with `QSep` in the data annotation lesson.

We can make the same plot for the SVM predictions by passing `fcol =
"svm.pred"` to `mrkConsProfiles`. Proteins left as `"unknown"` are not
included. We reuse the order from the markers so that the two plots can be
compared row by row. If the classification is sensible, the newly classified
proteins should keep the fingerprint of their compartment.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Consensus profiles of the SVM predictions, in the same order as the markers
fmat_svm <- mrkConsProfiles(msn, fcol = "svm.pred")
plotConsProfiles(fmat_svm, order = ord)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


The fingerprints of the predictions are usually a little less sharp than those
of the markers, because the classified proteins include proteins that lie
further from the centre of each compartment. A compartment whose fingerprint
changes markedly would be worth investigating further.


## Peptide support and missing values

All of the maps we have made so far treat each protein equally. However, some
proteins are quantified from many precursors, whilst others rely on only one
or two. Similarly, some profiles are complete, whereas others were partly
filled in by imputation. Proteins with little peptide support or many missing
values tend to have noisier profiles, which can place them between clusters on
a map or prevent them from being classified confidently. Overlaying this
information on our maps helps us to interpret them.

### Peptide support across the combined data

At the end of part 1 we added the number of precursors supporting
each protein in each replicate (`n_rep1`, `n_rep2`, `n_rep3`), together with
their minimum (`n_min`). We use the minimum because a protein is only as well
supported as its weakest replicate: a protein with 12, 10 and 1 precursors
has a reasonable mean, but its profile in the third replicate rests on a
single precursor.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Summary of the minimum number of precursors per protein
msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(n_min) |>
  summary()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   1.00    4.00    9.50   14.74   19.00  474.00 
```


:::
:::


We can show peptide support on a spatial map by scaling the size of each point.
The `plot2D` function accepts a vector of point sizes through its `cex`
argument. We use a log scale, so that the few proteins with very many
precursors do not dominate the plot.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Point size based on the (log) minimum number of precursors
ptsze <- 0.3 + log2(fData(msn)$n_min) / 3

plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", cex = ptsze,
       main = "PCA: SVM predictions, sized by peptide support")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "svm.pred", where = "topright", cex = .6)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


Large points are well supported proteins, and small points are proteins
supported by few precursors in at least one replicate. Look at where the small
points lie: are they spread evenly across the map, or concentrated in
particular regions, such as between clusters?

### Missing values across the combined data

We can do the same for missing values. The `missing_max` column gives, for
each protein, the largest proportion of values that were missing before
imputation in any one replicate. Again, a profile is only as reliable as its
weakest replicate.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Summary of the maximum proportion of missing values per protein
msn |>
  fData() |>
  pull(missing_max) |>
  summary()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.0000  0.3194  0.4444  0.4598  0.5926  0.7778 
```


:::
:::


This time we make points smaller as the proportion of missing values
increases, so that large points are still the most reliable proteins.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Point size decreases with the proportion of missing values
ptsze_na <- 1.5 * (1 - fData(msn)$missing_max)

plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", cex = ptsze_na,
       main = "PCA: SVM predictions, sized by completeness")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "svm.pred", where = "topright", cex = .6)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::



### Comparing compartments

We can now ask directly whether peptide support and missing values differ
between compartments, and in particular whether the proteins left as
`"unknown"` tend to be less reliable. We put both columns in long format and
plot them side by side.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Colours for each compartment, with unknown in grey
pred_cols <- c(setNames(getStockcol()[seq_along(getMarkerClasses(msn))],
                        getMarkerClasses(msn)),
               unknown = getUnknowncol())

## Peptide support and missing values per predicted compartment
msn |>
  fData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::select(svm.pred, n_min, missing_max) |>
  pivot_longer(-svm.pred, names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(measure = recode(measure,
                          n_min = "Minimum number of precursors",
                          missing_max = "Maximum proportion missing")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = svm.pred, y = value, fill = svm.pred)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pred_cols) +
  labs(x = "SVM prediction", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=1152}
:::
:::


The two measures are related: proteins with few precursors often have more
missing values, because there are fewer precursors to fill in the gaps. Look
at whether any compartment, or the `"unknown"` proteins, stand out on either
measure. Do you think this is biological or technical?

### Peptide support and missing values in each replicate

The minimum and maximum hide which replicate is responsible for a poorly
supported or incomplete profile. To see this, we return to the data of each
replicate in our `QFeatures` object, before the replicates were joined, as we
did in the lesson on assessing resolution. We coerce the normalised
protein-level set of each replicate to an `MSnSet`, and add the `.n` and
`prop_missing` columns that `addProfileQC()` stored in the protein-level sets
in part 1.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Normalised protein-level sets for each replicate, before joining
rep_sets <- c(rep1 = "proteins_norm_R1",
              rep2 = "proteins_norm_R2",
              rep3 = "proteins_norm_R3")

## Sets output by aggregateFeatures, which contain .n and prop_missing
agg_sets <- c(rep1 = "proteins_R1",
              rep2 = "proteins_R2",
              rep3 = "proteins_R3")

## One MSnSet per replicate, with its own peptide support and missing values
msn_reps <- lapply(names(rep_sets), function(r) {
  x <- as(qf[[rep_sets[r]]], "MSnSet")
  rd <- rowData(qf[[agg_sets[r]]])
  idx <- match(featureNames(x), rownames(rd))
  fData(x)$n <- rd$.n[idx]
  fData(x)$prop_missing <- rd$prop_missing[idx]
  x
})
names(msn_reps) <- names(rep_sets)

## Number of precursors and proportion missing per protein in each replicate
sapply(msn_reps, function(x) summary(fData(x)$n))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
             rep1      rep2      rep3
Min.      1.00000   1.00000   1.00000
1st Qu.   5.00000   5.00000   4.00000
Median   10.00000  10.00000  10.00000
Mean     15.65868  15.86315  15.27169
3rd Qu.  20.00000  21.00000  20.00000
Max.    474.00000 629.00000 636.00000
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sapply(msn_reps, function(x) summary(fData(x)$prop_missing))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
             rep1      rep2      rep3
Min.    0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000
1st Qu. 0.2037037 0.3055556 0.2802676
Median  0.3111111 0.4333333 0.4027778
Mean    0.3488944 0.4472738 0.4247754
3rd Qu. 0.4814815 0.5833333 0.5555556
Max.    0.7777778 0.7777778 0.7777778
```


:::
:::


Our classification was carried out on the combined data. To colour the
replicate maps, we copy the SVM predictions across by matching protein
accessions. Proteins that were not part of the combined data (for example,
because they were missing from another replicate) are labelled `"unknown"`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Copy the SVM predictions from the combined data to each replicate
for (r in names(msn_reps)) {
  ids <- featureNames(msn_reps[[r]])
  pred <- fData(msn)[ids, "svm.pred"]
  pred[is.na(pred)] <- "unknown"
  fData(msn_reps[[r]])$svm.pred <- pred
}
```
:::


We can now plot each replicate, with points sized by that replicate's peptide
support. To size the points by completeness instead, replace the `cex`
argument with `1.5 * (1 - fData(msn_reps[[r]])$prop_missing)`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (r in names(msn_reps)) {
  plot2D(msn_reps[[r]], fcol = "svm.pred",
         cex = 0.3 + log2(fData(msn_reps[[r]])$n) / 3,
         main = paste("PCA:", r))
}
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_04_features_of_interest_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=1440}
:::
:::


Each replicate has its own PCA, so the plots may be rotated or mirrored
relative to each other. What matters is that the same structure appears in
each. Plotting replicates separately in this way is also a useful check that
the replicates agree, and that no single replicate has noticeably lower peptide
support, more missing values or poorer resolution than the others.

::: {.callout-exercise}

## Overlaying protein complexes

Users may wish to add further information to their maps, for example protein
complexes, pathways of interest, or compartments that were not used as
training data because they lacked resolution or had too few marker proteins.
Protein complexes are a particularly nice example, because their members are
expected to be found together, and related complexes can reveal how finely
our data resolves the cell.

### Finding complex members by gene name

To find the members of a complex, it is convenient to search the feature data
by gene name. Our data contains a column of gene names from DIA-NN (here
`Genes`; check `fvarLabels(msn)` for the name in your data). Where several
genes map to the same protein group, they are separated by a semicolon, so we
write a small helper function that splits these and searches each gene name
against a pattern.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Return the proteins whose gene name(s) match a regular expression
find_genes <- function(object, pattern, gcol = "Genes") {
  genes <- strsplit(as.character(fData(object)[[gcol]]), ";")
  hit <- vapply(genes, function(g) any(grepl(pattern, g)), logical(1))
  featureNames(object)[hit]
}
```
:::


The `pattern` is a regular expression. For example, `"^ATP6V1"` matches all
gene names starting with `ATP6V1`, and `"^(TCP1|CCT[2-8][AB]?)$"` matches
`TCP1` and `CCT2` to `CCT8` (including `CCT6A` and `CCT6B`) exactly. You can
also use the `pRolocVis` app (`pRolocVis(msn, fcol = "svm.pred")`) to search
the feature data interactively.

### A well-behaved complex: the TRiC chaperonin

The TRiC (or CCT) chaperonin is a large cytosolic complex of eight different
subunits that helps newly made proteins to fold. We expect its subunits to be
found together, making it a good first example.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Members of the TRiC chaperonin
tric <- find_genes(msn, "^(TCP1|CCT[2-8][AB]?)$")
fData(msn)[tric, c("Genes", "svm.pred")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
       Genes     svm.pred
P17987  TCP1      unknown
P40227 CCT6A      unknown
P48643  CCT5      unknown
P49368  CCT3      unknown
P50990  CCT8      unknown
P50991  CCT4      unknown
P78371  CCT2      unknown
Q99832  CCT7 Ribosome 40S
```


:::
:::


We can highlight these proteins on any map using `highlightOnPlot`. We first
draw the map with `plot2D`, and then pass the same coordinates and our
proteins of interest (`foi`, features of interest) to `highlightOnPlot`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "PCA: TRiC chaperonin")
highlightOnPlot(pcas, foi = tric, col = "black", bg = "yellow",
                pch = 21, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)

plot2D(tsne, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "svm.pred", main = "t-SNE: TRiC chaperonin")
highlightOnPlot(tsne, foi = tric, col = "black", bg = "yellow",
                pch = 21, cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)
```

The map shows *where* the complex lies. To see *why*, we can compare the
profiles of its members with those of the cytosolic markers using `plotDist`.
The `markers` argument tells `plotDist` which proteins to highlight, here the
TRiC subunits in black, while the cytosolic markers are plotted in grey.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Cytosol markers
cyto_markers <- featureNames(msn)[fData(msn)$markers == "Cytosol"]

## TRiC subunits (black) on top of the cytosol markers (grey)
plotDist(msn[c(cyto_markers, tric), ],
         markers = tric, type = "l",
         mcol = "black", pcol = "grey",
         las = 2)
title("TRiC subunits (black) and cytosol markers (grey)")
```

### Related complexes in different places: the adaptor complexes

The adaptor protein (AP) complexes select cargo for vesicle transport. They
are closely related, but act in different places: AP-2 at the plasma membrane,
AP-1 at the Golgi and endosomes, and AP-3 at endosomes. Can our data
distinguish them?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Members of the AP-1, AP-2 and AP-3 complexes
ap1 <- find_genes(msn, "^AP1[BGMS]")
ap2 <- find_genes(msn, "^AP2[ABMS]")
ap3 <- find_genes(msn, "^AP3[BDMS]")

lengths(list(AP1 = ap1, AP2 = ap2, AP3 = ap3))
```

### Adding complexes as a new `fData` column

Alternatively, we can store our annotations in a new column of the feature
data, just as we did for markers. This keeps the annotation with the data and
allows us to use all the usual plotting functions. The easiest way is to
create a named vector, with the annotation as values and the protein
accessions as names, and add it with `addMarkers`. All proteins not in the
vector are labelled `"unknown"`.

As an example, we look at the vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase), the proton pump that
acidifies lysosomes and endosomes. It has two parts: V0, which sits in the
membrane, and V1, which assembles onto V0 from the cytosol and can come off
again. Do the two parts sit in the same place on our map?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## V-ATPase V1 and V0 subunits
v1 <- find_genes(msn, "^ATP6V1")
v0 <- find_genes(msn, "^ATP6V0")

## Named vector of annotations
vatpase <- c(setNames(rep("V-ATPase V1", length(v1)), v1),
             setNames(rep("V-ATPase V0", length(v0)), v0))

## Add as a new fData column called "vatpase"
msn <- addMarkers(msn, markers = vatpase, mcol = "vatpase")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Markers in data: 13 out of 8736
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
organelleMarkers
    unknown V-ATPase V0 V-ATPase V1 
       8723           5           8 
```


:::
:::


We can now pass this column to `fcol` to plot a map in which only the
V-ATPase subunits are coloured.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot2D(pcas, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "vatpase", cex = 1.5, main = "PCA: V-ATPase")
addLegend(msn, fcol = "vatpase", where = "topleft", cex = .8)
plot2D(tsne, method = "none", methargs = list(msn),
       fcol = "vatpase", cex = 1.5, main = "t-SNE: V-ATPase")
```

The same approach can be used for any annotation, for example proteins from a
pathway of interest, proteins identified in another experiment, or a
compartment that was not included in the training data.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

* Spatial maps of classification results are made with `plot2D` by passing
  the prediction column to `fcol`. Different dimensionality reduction methods
  show the data in different ways, so it is good practice to look at more
  than one.
* Pre-computing coordinates with `plot = FALSE`, using a seed for stochastic
  methods, and reusing them with `method = "none"` makes figures faster and
  reproducible.
* `mrkConsProfiles` calculates the consensus profile, or fingerprint, of each
  compartment, and `plotConsProfiles` displays them as a heatmap, ordered by
  similarity using `mrkHClust`.
* Peptide support and missing values can be shown on spatial maps by scaling
  point size. Proteins supported by few precursors, or with many values
  imputed, tend to have noisier profiles, so these measures help to interpret
  their position on the map and their classification. Plotting replicates
  separately shows which replicate is responsible.
* Members of protein complexes can be found by gene name, highlighted on any
  map with `highlightOnPlot`, and stored as new `fData` columns with
  `addMarkers`. Comparing their profiles with those of their compartment
  using `plotDist` shows why they lie where they do.
:::
